39: Paella is easy for a client to search for and hard to pull off well at an event. According to DataForSEO (October 2026), people in the U.S. search "spanish catering" about 2,900 times a month, "paella catering" and "paella caterer" about 720 times each, "paella party" about 320 times and "tapas catering" about 140 times. Those are buyers, not future owners: the person who wants to start the business searches "paella business" about 10 times a month. Demand comes from families planning backyard paella parties, couples booking weddings and rehearsal dinners, and companies ordering team lunches and holiday parties. This plan is for a paella chef who wants to serve all three without running a restaurant. We prep in a permitted commissary, then cook the paella live at the client's venue.
40: The concept is a live paella caterer. The paella is cooked in front of the guests, in pans of 26 to 36 in (65 to 90 cm) over 3-ring propane burners, and served with a salad and bread. That cooking is the product, not an extra: guests watch the sofrito go in, the stock go on and the socarrat form. The sofrito, the stock, the cut vegetables and the cleaned seafood come out of the commissary the day before, so at the event we only cook and serve. Drop-off paella, cooked in the commissary and delivered hot, is the smaller second line, and a seafood and tapas premium is the third. Gas is the base; wood only where a permit allows it, and induction indoors. We are not a paella food truck or a restaurant.
41: The total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} in startup costs plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The heaviest lines are the used cargo van ({{inv_furgoneta}}), the paella pans ({{inv_paelleras}}), the burners and stands ({{inv_quemadores}}) and the launch budget ({{inv_lanzamiento}}). Notice how small the cooking gear is next to the van. We do not build or lease a restaurant, which keeps the investment well below a venue with its own dining room and kitchen. We cover it with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. A loan of that size does not fit the $50,000 SBA Microloan cap, so the realistic routes are a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, and no plan can promise a lender's answer.
42: In year 1 we plan {{eventos_a1}} events with an average of {{invitados_evento}} guests at {{precio_invitado}} per guest, excluding sales tax. That adds up to {{ventas_a1}} in revenue, growing to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3 as events rise to {{eventos_a2}} and {{eventos_a3}}. Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, the lowest debt service coverage is {{dscr_min}}, and the business breaks even at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events a year. Be honest about what this case is: a full-time owner who is also the paella chef, with a second cook on weekends, not the average first year. A new operator more often lands near $225,000 in sales in year 1 (a kit estimate), so read these numbers as a well-run target and change the inputs to your own.
43: The founding team is small. The owner is the paella chef, who also sells and buys. A lead cook, who doubles as the second paella chef, covers the second pan line on busy weekends, event staff (servers and buffet attendants) work event by event, and a prep cook doubles as the van driver. Everyone except the owner is a part-time hourly W-2 employee. That makes {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents. Replace this paragraph with your own background: a lender wants to see who has run a rice kitchen and who has sold events. The plan shows that a paella caterer can start without a restaurant and with controlled risk, as long as every event is quoted, deposited and staffed on purpose.
46: Our clients buy an event that goes well, not just rice. Families book backyard paella parties, birthdays, first communions, baptisms and quinceaneras, and want one person to handle the menu, the timeline and the cleanup. Couples book weddings and rehearsal dinners months ahead and want the paella pan, the socarrat and the tasting to feel personal. Companies, usually through an office manager or a planner, want live cooking for a team event or hot drop-off lunches, with an invoice that fits company rules. A smaller premium group pays for seafood and tapas. All of them want the rice at its best when the guests sit down, no logistics to think about and a quote with no surprises. The sales cycle differs: couples book once, companies reorder.
47: Our value proposition rests on three pillars. First, the show: paella "cooked live in front of your guests in a giant traditional pan," as one Florida operator puts it on Zola. The sofrito, the stock and the golden socarrat reveal are explained by the person cooking, and that moment is sold as an experience, not just a plate. Second, the product: imported bomba rice, saffron, and sofrito and stock made the day before, so the pan at the event is about assembly and timing, not improvisation. Third, reliability: allergens written into every quote, a tasting before the contract, arrival with time to spare and a paella chef included in the price, while some operators bill the paella chef separately (a San Diego restaurant caterer lists $300 for two hours). Each pillar lets us compete on the experience and stay out of the price war over the cheapest tray.
48: We quote by the guest, excluding sales tax and with the paella chef, the staff and the service charge included, and the average is {{precio_invitado}}. With {{invitados_evento}} guests per event, the average event brings in {{ventas_evento}}. Paella packages are {{cuota_paquetes_pct}} of sales, and the rest are add-ons such as a tapas hour, desserts, non-alcoholic sangria and drinks, rentals, extra hours and travel fees. A guest minimum protects small events (the operators we read ask for 20 to 30 guests), and a deposit blocks the date: most US caterers ask for 25% to 50% (a kit estimate), and the pricing calculator proposes 50%. The service charge is part of our price. A voluntary gratuity is not, and it belongs to the staff.
49: We compete against four alternatives. Spanish restaurants that cater on the side have a name and good food, but their kitchen serves the dining room first. General caterers put paella on the menu as one more dish and rarely cook it live. Other paella caterers sell a similar show, and the best of them are booked on the same Saturdays we want. Grocery trays win on price for small orders and lose on service. Paella food trucks sell a different product, a quick line at a brewery or a lot, so we do not compete with them on speed. We place ourselves in the gap: paella cooked live, a price that includes the paella chef, seafood from an approved source and one person responsible for the event from the quote to the cleanup. We compete on the experience, not on the cheapest tray.
50: Three packages let the client match the event to the budget: drop-off paella, delivered hot from the commissary; a live paella party, with the pan cooked on site, salad and bread; and a full-service live paella with staff and a buffet. A tapas hour is a switch that can be added to any of them. Eight menu styles give the paella chef something to sell: seafood, chicken and seafood, chicken and chorizo, Valencian (rabbit on request), farm vegetable (vegan), paella negra, lobster and seafood as the premium, and an easy-eat peeled seafood version, with fideua (noodle paella) as a menu note. We sell them for backyard paella parties, weddings with a tapas hour, corporate live cooking, rehearsal dinners, first communions, baptisms, quinceaneras and birthdays. Each package has a guest minimum, because small events do not cover the cook and the crew. The pricing calculator builds each quote from your own costs.
53: Demand for paella catering comes from the buyer, and search data shows it. According to DataForSEO (October 2026), people in the U.S. search "spanish catering" about 2,900 times a month, "paella catering" about 720 times, "paella party" about 320 times and "tapas catering" about 140 times. Related searches include "paella catering cost", "paella catering menu" and "paella catering near me". These are people who want to hire a caterer, not start one, so they confirm that demand exists without giving us a market size, which we do not quote because every source defines it differently. What matters for you is local: how many venues, offices, wedding planners and Spanish-speaking communities sit within an hour of your commissary.
54: Private clients are the most emotional buyers: weddings, rehearsal dinners, birthdays and family milestones. They compare photos, reviews and the price per person before they ask for a quote. As a reference, a Southwest Florida operator lists live paella with salad and bread at $12 to $13 a plate on Zola, while Taste of Paella in Miami lists $26 to $31 per person and $45 for lobster, with a 25-guest minimum in peak season. On WeddingWire, a San Francisco operator says couples usually spend $50. The example prices weddings at $52 per guest, in line with that range, and the tasting and the contract help defend it. In Florida the peak season runs from winter into spring; set your own prices from local quotes.
55: Corporate clients buy on a different logic. They book live cooking for team events, openings and holiday parties, and hot drop-off lunches for meetings and training days. The buyer is usually an office manager or a planner who needs a reliable vendor and an invoice that fits company rules. As a reference, full Spanish menus with staff run from about $44 per guest at Señor Pepe's on Zola to $65 at Miami Grill Catering, which doubles its minimum in the end-of-year holiday season. Many companies order through corporate catering marketplaces such as ezCater, which the example models at {{marketplace_pct}} of sales with a {{marketplace_comision}} commission. December holiday parties fill the calendar around them.
56: The example mix is a kit estimate, not market data. Of {{eventos_a1}} events, 25 are corporate drop-offs (30 guests at $22), 60 are backyard paella parties (45 guests at $34), 25 are company events (75 guests at $38), 18 are weddings and rehearsal dinners (110 guests at $52) and 7 are seafood and tapas premium events (70 guests at $65). Weddings are 13% of the events and 33% of the sales. The calendar is uneven too. The example opens in March, so Month 1 is March, with the peaks in May, June and October and the weakest months in January and February. The lowest cash balance falls in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}} at {{saldo_minimo}}. Rotate the curve to your opening month and replace the shares with what your bookings show.
57: A few trends are worth watching, without leaning on numbers we cannot source. Spanish food and tapas keep gaining ground on wedding menus, and live cooking gives guests something to watch. Sangria bars and flamenco guitar show up in the listings we read, though selling alcohol takes a license, so many operators offer non-alcoholic options. Clients also ask more often for gluten-free, vegetarian and allergy-safe options, and expect the caterer to handle them without drama.
58: Demand has risks the plan should name. The season is short, so a slow spring can leave a gap that fall may not fill. Clients cancel or cut the guest count late, which is why the deposit and the cancellation terms matter. Wind and rain can move a cooking station, and a burn ban or a fire marshal's call can rule out open flame on the day, so wood is only a bonus. Seafood prices swing too. And {{eventos_a1}} events a year is the pace of a full-time owner-paella chef with a second cook on weekends, not of a typical first year. The pessimistic scenario shows the hit: {{pesimista_eventos}} events and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}, and the cash runs out.
61: Before you set a price, map who competes with you within an hour of your commissary. The list usually includes other paella caterers (Taste of Paella, Señor Pepe's and Miami Grill Catering are examples we read), Spanish restaurants that cater, general caterers with a Spanish menu, grocery trays and paella food trucks that book private events. For each one, note what the price per guest includes, its guest minimum, whether it cooks on site and what its reviews say. You do not need invented figures: request quotes and read their websites and their reviews on Google and The Knot.
62: Porter's five forces look like this for a paella caterer. Supplier power is low to moderate: many seafood purveyors, rice importers and equipment dealers compete for your order, although seafood and saffron prices swing and a single supplier can raise your costs. Buyer power is moderate: clients compare quotes and reviews, but a good tasting and a clear proposal build loyalty, and corporate accounts push harder on price. The threat of substitutes is real: a Spanish restaurant's catering menu, a grocery tray, a paella food truck or a friend with a big pan can replace you on a lower budget. Rivalry peaks in May, June and October, when everyone chases the same Saturdays. The threat of new entrants is moderate: a pan and a burner are easy to buy, but cooking well for 40 guests per pan, a permitted commissary, insurance that covers open flame, a propane setup that passes the fire marshal and the cash for a van take planning, and that slows the hobbyists.
63: Direct competitors are paella caterers and Spanish restaurants that cook for the same event sizes and the same venues, from weekend operators to full-service companies. Indirect ones are grocery and big-box trays, general caterers with a Spanish menu and the family that cooks a big pan at home. To compare fairly, line up the price per guest, what it includes (the paella chef, staff, dishes and flatware, a travel fee, which one San Diego caterer includes up to a 20 mile radius), the guest minimum, whether they cook on site and their reviews on The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola and Google. Some operators bill the paella chef separately, at $300 for two hours in one San Diego restaurant's case. Then decide where you win: the live cooking, the menu styles, the speed of your reply or the clarity of your proposal. Put it in one sentence and use it everywhere.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. You need a permitted commissary kitchen, because there is no legal way to sell food prepared at home. Cooking at the event usually counts as a food establishment under the FDA Food Code, and some counties have a lighter category for limited food preparation (San Diego County is one example), so ask your county. Then add the gear: a 36 in (90 cm) paella pan runs about $349 and a 3-ring burner about $549 (kit estimates based on retail listings), and the example budgets {{inv_paelleras}} for pans and {{inv_quemadores}} for burners. Add insurance that does not exclude open flame, your fire marshal's rules on propane and cooking tents, and the craft of a paella chef who can get a golden socarrat for 40 guests every weekend.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is reliability: arriving with time to spare, with the guest count agreed and the paella hot at service. The second is food safety. Cooked rice is a time and temperature control food and a known source of Bacillus cereus, so serve it at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, or hold it under a written time as a public health control procedure for up to 4 hours, and throw leftovers away. Cook to the FDA Food Code minimums: 165 °F (74 °C) for chicken, 145 °F (63 °C) for 15 seconds for fish and shellfish and 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds for raw Mexican-style chorizo; Spanish cured chorizo is ready to eat. The third is a consistent socarrat, which is quality, not safety. The fourth is your relationship with venues and wedding planners, who send many bookings. A small caterer that does all four well can take work from larger rivals.
66: The SWOT for this concept looks like this. Strengths: low fixed costs, since you pay {{ocupacion_anual}} a year for a commissary and equipment storage instead of a restaurant lease, a live show that people already search for, and a mix of five demand lines. Weaknesses: reliance on a few key people, limited capacity on the busiest Saturdays (the plan allows up to {{capacidad_eventos}} events a year with one van and one crew), an uneven calendar and a tight margin of safety. Opportunities: companies that want a regular vendor, venues and planners with preferred vendor lists, and families who return for the next celebration. Threats: a foodborne illness, a propane or fire incident, wind and rain, burn bans, late cancellations, volatile seafood prices and cheap paella-only offers.
69: The marketing strategy follows two funnels, plus one channel that runs on referrals. Weddings and rehearsal dinners have a long cycle: the client finds you online, asks for a quote, attends a tasting and signs months before the date. Companies have a short, repeating cycle: a well-run team lunch leads to the next order and to a referral inside the same office. Backyard paella parties travel by word of mouth, so treat each funnel with its own message and channel. Rest all of them on the same promise: paella cooked live that arrives at its best, a paella chef the guests can see and a contract that gives peace of mind.
70: Your website is the main sales tool, because clients read it before they call. It should show the menu styles, "starting at" prices per guest for each type of event, photos of real events and a short quote form that asks for the date, the venue, the guest count and allergies. Add an FAQ that answers what people search for: how many guests a 36 in (90 cm) pan serves, how much rice to plan per person, what paella catering costs and whether you can cook paella at home and sell it. Complete your Google Business Profile and keep collecting recent reviews, so you show up when someone searches "paella catering", a phrase with about 720 searches a month. Instagram and TikTok videos of the paella cooking and the socarrat reveal sell more than any slogan.
71: Directories bring qualified leads when your profile is complete. For weddings, The Knot, WeddingWire and Zola are where couples compare vendors, read reviews and request quotes. Thumbtack suits parties and smaller events, where you pay for leads and need to reply fast. For companies, ezCater lists you for office orders and takes a commission, which the workbook models at {{marketplace_comision}} of the sales that come through it. Add LinkedIn and direct outreach to office managers and planners. Some venues charge an outside vendor fee, so price it into the quote before you accept. Use the directories to win new clients, and invite repeat clients to book directly.
72: Direct selling works if you are willing to go out and meet people. Start with the venues, wedding planners and office managers in your area, and bring a one-page sheet with the menu styles, the packages and a starting price per guest. Ask to be added to a venue's preferred vendor list: a venue that recommends you sends bookings at no advertising cost. Reach out to the Hispanic community too, through parishes, event halls and families planning first communions and quinceaneras. Offer a live tasting to the planners who book the most, since someone who has seen you cook recommends you with more confidence. Bridal shows let you meet couples in person. After every visit, send an email and set a reminder. A steady rhythm of small contacts each week works better than one big campaign.
73: The tasting is the step closest to the sale, so budget it as a line in the plan (the P&L carries it as tastings for prospects). Offer it to serious prospects, mainly couples and companies with big events, as a small paella cooked live and a printed proposal. You can charge for it and credit it to the contract if the client signs. The proposal lists the menu, the guest count, the staff, the price per guest and the guest minimum. Ask for a deposit to hold the date (the calculator proposes 50%), with the balance due before the event. Companies often pay on net 30 terms, while the workbook assumes you collect in {{cobro_dias}} days on average, since private clients pay before the date. Follow up within a day.
74: The best marketing comes after the event. Ask for a Google review within a few days, while the client still remembers the party, and send a short thank-you with a photo if they agree. Companies that reorder get a simple process: their usual menu saved and one named contact. Ask happy clients to introduce you to a friend planning a birthday or a colleague who books team lunches, and thank them with a small gesture. Families that book one celebration often return for the next one. A referral habit run well costs less than any new lead.
75: The example reserves {{marketing_anual}} a year for marketing, mostly for The Knot and WeddingWire listings, Google Ads, Thumbtack leads, photography and bridal shows, plus the launch budget, which is already in the investment. Record where each lead comes from (website, directory, venue, planner, referral or ezCater) and calculate the marketing cost per event won. If a channel wins events at a lower cost, it gets more budget; if not, drop it. Review the numbers every quarter and adjust.
